<reason>Both sides were sharp, aphoristic, and disciplined about not inventing sources. PRO built the cleaner decision rule: a dating app's output is a private meeting, so the question is whether a removal can be made to stick, and whether the anonymity CON defends is symmetrical. CON's best counter — stolen documents and rented faces mean the file may name an innocent — genuinely damaged PRO's "morning after" story for industrial fraud, and the honeypot/exclusion harms stayed live. But CON never resolved the asymmetry that a rented face cannot show up on the date, so its answer works far better against scam farms than against the banned abuser who is PRO's central harm. CON also conceded the direction on cost ("Yes, the price rises"), which PRO pressed hard, and CON's late list of substitutes (phone numbers, device fingerprints, photo hashes, cards) was persuasively reframed by PRO as purchasable objects versus a non-restockable face. CON's Q2 pressure on the motion-as-written was legitimate and PRO's "yes, as written, and competent verification includes document variety and appeal" answer was adequate rather than airtight, so the gap stays competitive. PRO's fixable-harms versus structural-harms ledger, plus the "who bears the risk" frame, gave the easier vote. PRO's closing being clipped for overlength is a real execution cost that trims the margin.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 sequence: after CON initially left "what stops a banned man returning that evening" unanswered, CON supplied phone numbers, device fingerprints, photo hashes and payment cards, and PRO's closing recast all four as items "you can buy again on the way home" — a toll booth, not a wall — leaving the face as the only non-restockable credential. CON's counter that a rented face is also bought never addressed that a rented face cannot appear at the date.</best_rebuttal>
